d368103041.what_happened: The United States has lost its measles-free status, 26 years after the disease was declared eliminated there, as the country battles its highest measles case count in more than 30 years. Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each announced one additional measles-associated death on Friday, bringing the total to 10 deaths this year. Federal and state officials are now disputing how measles deaths should be counted.
details: The United States has lost its measles-free status, 26 years after measles was declared eliminated there in 2000, US media reported. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked the status, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, after determining uninterrupted measles transmission for more than 12 months. More than 5,400 confirmed cases have been recorded to date, per CDC and Johns Hopkins University International Vaccine Access Center tracker data, with cases as of November 2026 more than double the 2,289 confirmed in 2025.

Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each announced one additional measles-associated death on Friday, marking 10 total US deaths linked to the disease this year. Wisconsin's Department of Health Services reported an infant's death, while Pennsylvania's Department of Health said its latest death was an unvaccinated patient who tested positive for measles. Pennsylvania has logged seven measles-associated deaths and Wisconsin two, and on November 2 New York said a child died in the state's first recorded measles death in more than 30 years.

Al Jazeera reports about 7,500 people infected and 13 deaths since last year, a period coinciding with the tenure of Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has for years spread doubts without scientific evidence about measles vaccine safety. The CDC recorded six measles-related deaths, twice its 2025 figure, but its national toll is lower than state-reported numbers after Kennedy asked CDC director Erica Schwartz not to count the deaths, claiming no evidence they were measles-associated. The count is at the centre of a dispute between Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Kennedy; Pennsylvania counts a death as measles-associated when a confirmed case dies within 30 days of symptoms, unless it resulted from an unrelated event.

The CDC says it is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists on a standardised definition for measles deaths, but infectious disease experts warn the dispute puts the agency at odds with longstanding tracking practice used by the WHO and CDC. Vaccination coverage among US kindergarteners fell from 95.2 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025-2026, and local and state health departments have ramped up vaccination efforts. Measles is preventable through the MMR vaccine, which offers about 97 percent protection after two doses; Canada, Spain and the United Kingdom recently lost elimination status after a WHO expert review, and the US left the WHO but remains a PAHO member.
d368103041.why_it_matters: Measles is highly contagious and preventable, and losing elimination status after 26 years follows the highest case numbers in more than 30 years amid falling kindergarten vaccination coverage.
key_facts: US lost measles-free status, 26 years after elimination in 2000, PAHO ruled after 12 months' transmission.
Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each announced one more measles death Friday, reaching 10 deaths this year.
Pennsylvania: seven deaths; Wisconsin: two; New York child died November 2, first state death in 30 years.
Over 5,400 confirmed cases, more than double 2025's 2,289; Al Jazeera reports 7,500 infected, 13 dead.
CDC counts six deaths; Kennedy asked director Erica Schwartz not to count others, citing no evidence.
Pennsylvania counts deaths within 30 days of symptoms; CDC drafting standardised definition with epidemiologists' council.
Kindergarten vaccination coverage fell from 95.2 percent in 2019-2020 to 92.4 percent in 2025-2026.
MMR vaccine gives about 97 percent protection after two doses; Canada, Spain, UK also lost status.
d368103041.whats_next: The CDC is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to establish a standardised definition for measles deaths, and local and state health departments have ramped up vaccination efforts.
d368103041.blurb: The US has lost its measles-free status after 26 years, as cases hit 30-year highs and 10 deaths are reported this year.
d368103041.spoken: Good evening, here is your health news. The United States has lost its measles-free status, 26 years after the disease was declared eliminated there in 2000. The Pan American Health Organization took the step after measles spread without interruption for more than 12 months, as the country faces its highest case numbers in over 30 years. Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each announced another death on Friday, bringing this year's toll to 10, including an infant in Wisconsin. More than 5,400 cases are confirmed, over double the 2,289 reported in 2025. Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr disputes how deaths are counted, while the CDC works on a standard definition. Vaccination coverage among kindergarteners has fallen, and health departments are boosting vaccination efforts.
d368103041.subject: Measles outbreak

02c39fc805.what_happened: An Israeli air strike killed Hamas commander Samir Abu Younis in Khan Younis, southern Gaza on Saturday. The strike hit a tent sheltering displaced people, wounding two others. Israeli forces said the target was a senior Hamas military commander.
details: Hamas confirmed that Rafah brigade commander Samir Abu Younis was killed in an Israeli air strike on the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza on Saturday. Israel's military and Shin Bet said in a joint statement they targeted a senior Hamas military commander in a drone strike in Khan Younis on Saturday. The strike hit a tent sheltering displaced people, wounding two others, and casualties were taken to Nasser Medical Complex.

Gaza's Ministry of Health said on Saturday that Israeli attacks killed 16 people and injured 68 others over the past 48 hours. Since the ceasefire took effect on October 11, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,643 Palestinians and injured 5,964, with at least 850 bodies recovered from under the rubble. Since the war began in October 2023, at least 74,695 people have been killed and 176,093 injured, according to the Health Ministry, which also reported 11 deaths related to cold, including a nine-month-old baby who died from hypothermia.

Al-Mawasi, a coastal strip on the Mediterranean, is crowded with displaced Palestinians living in tents; Israel has repeatedly attacked the area despite previously designating it a humanitarian zone. Gaza's residents, most of whom have been displaced, are living in tents and damaged buildings as water damage from recent heavy rains has set in. Israeli attacks have escalated across Gaza despite the October ceasefire.

37af75b554.what_happened: Saudi-led coalition forces intercepted two ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh early Sunday, following the interception of two drones in Riyadh and southern regions on Saturday. The coalition also intercepted several drones aimed at Yemen's Marib city. Fighting intensified across multiple Yemeni governorates with heavy casualties and displacements reported.
details: On Sunday, coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki posted on X that air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward Riyadh. On Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones were intercepted and destroyed in the Riyadh and southern regions.

Saudi authorities say at least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in the kingdom since September 23. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh's King Khalid International airport, the East-West pipeline, and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia. The coalition also said it intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.

Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces made gains against the Houthis in al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf as fighting intensified in Marib. He said 321 Houthi leaders were killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group were destroyed. The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes, 56 drone attacks, and 541 artillery strikes.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Saudi-led coalition launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours. Saree said the Houthis targeted Yemen's Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles. Houthi-affiliated media reported two women and two children injured from artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa. More than 340,000 people have been displaced since August according to the International Organization for Migration. The US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans to exercise heightened vigilance, citing increased threat of Houthi attacks on civilian airports and critical infrastructure causing civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions, warning hostilities could spread rapidly.
key_facts: Coalition intercepted two ballistic missiles toward Riyadh Sunday
Two drones intercepted in Riyadh and southern regions Saturday
At least 26 killed in Houthi attacks since September 23

Yemeni army claims 321 Houthi leaders killed or wounded in 723 operations
Coalition conducted 37 air strikes, 56 drone attacks, 541 artillery strikes
Houthis report 72 coalition air strikes in past 24 hours

37af75b554.blurb: Saudi coalition intercepts missiles and drones targeting Riyadh as Yemen fighting escalates, displacing 340,000 and prompting US security alert.
37af75b554.spoken: Good morning. The Saudi-led coalition says it shot down two ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh early Sunday, just a day after it intercepted two drones over Riyadh and southern areas. Spokesperson Turki al-Maliki made both announcements. Since September, at least 26 people have died in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, including strikes on the capital's airport and oil facilities. The coalition also stopped several drones headed for the Yemeni city of Marib. Meanwhile, heavy fighting rages across several Yemeni governorates. Government forces claim gains in al-Jawf and say they've killed or wounded 321 Houthi leaders and destroyed 117 vehicles. The coalition carried out dozens of air and drone strikes and hundreds of artillery rounds. The Houthis say they faced 72 air strikes in the past day and fired missiles at government troops in Lahij. Houthi media report two women and two children hurt by shelling in Sanaa. Over 340,000 people have fled their homes since August. The US Embassy in Riyadh has warned Americans to stay alert, saying Houthi attacks on airports have caused casualties and travel chaos, and the conflict could spread quickly.
37af75b554.subject: Yemen conflict

f2630e293c.what_happened: The Consumer Affairs Authority (CAA) has summoned officials of LAUGFS Gas to explain a sharp increase in domestic gas prices. The company raised cylinder prices from midnight on November 13, with the 12.5kg cylinder up by Rs. 1,775 and the 5kg cylinder up by Rs. 732. LAUGFS blamed rising international market prices and higher shipping and insurance costs.
details: The Consumer Affairs Authority (CAA) has summoned officials of LAUGFS Gas to explain the recent sharp increase in domestic gas prices. The company's representatives have been instructed to appear before the Authority at 10.00 a.m. tomorrow, November 16, and provide explanations about the price revision.

LAUGFS Gas increased the prices of its domestic gas cylinders with effect from midnight on November 13. The price of a 12.5kg domestic gas cylinder went up by Rs. 1,775, from Rs. 4,965 to Rs. 6,740, while the price of a 5kg cylinder rose by Rs. 732, from Rs. 1,988 to Rs. 2,720.

The company attributed the price revision to rising international market prices and increased shipping and insurance costs, which it said had raised the cost of procuring bulk gas supplies for Sri Lanka. The CAA summoned the company officials to seek clarification regarding the reasons for the increase.

Company representatives must appear before the CAA at 10.00 a.m. tomorrow, November 16.

3485f8c799.what_happened: More than 350,000 Czechs rallied in Prague on Sunday against government plans to scrap the licence fees that fund public broadcasters. Organisers called it one of the biggest protests in the country's history. Protesters say the plan would give ministers more control over newsrooms and cut broadcaster budgets by about 15%.
details: Organisers said more than 350,000 people joined the Sunday rally in Prague, one of the largest in Czech history, to defend the mandatory licence fees that pay for Czechia's public broadcasters. It took place at Letná Plain, the cradle of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that ended more than 40 years of communist rule. Many wore triangular paper hats like Večerníček, a children's bedtime TV mascot that became the protest's symbol, and banners said the media would not be given away.

The plan would end the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7) a month, and pay for broadcasters from the state budget instead. Protesters say that would hand ministers more leverage over newsrooms, and the changes would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%. The bill's first reading was pushed through in the middle of the night in late October, and since then there have been repeated protests, weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities, and a strike by Czech TV and Czech Radio staff.

The Million Moments for Democracy group organised the rally and demanded the government drop the plan, warning that Babiš and his coalition partners threaten democracy. Lead organiser Mikuláš Minář said the rally was extraordinary and only the beginning. Singer Šárka Dumišincová said the media meant freedom to her, while computer programmer Jan Snasel said the government was trying to control the media, cut their funding and influence what they broadcast; banners rejected the Slovak scenario and told the government to keep its hands off the media.

The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute also criticised the plan, comparing it to steps by Slovakia's prime minister Robert Fico and Hungary's former premier Viktor Orbán; protesters cited Hungary, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia as places where rightwing populist governments weakened media independence. Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said protesters were stirring up the public with unfounded claims, wrote an op-ed about the opposition's seven lies over the fees, and said anyone talking about nationalisation was lying deliberately and that the government would never interfere in editorial work. His coalition includes his ANO movement, the rightwing Motorists for Themselves and the anti-migrant, pro-Russian Freedom and Direct Democracy party, and ANO still has about 30% support in opinion polls.
3485f8c799.why_it_matters: Protesters and international media groups say scrapping licence fees would let ministers control public newsrooms, eroding media independence as they say happened in Hungary, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia.
key_facts: Over 350,000 people rallied in Prague on Sunday to protect public broadcasting licence fees.
Government plans to scrap licence fees and fund Czech TV and radio from the state budget.
The changes would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%.
Licence fees together add up to 205 koruna (£7) a month.

3485f8c799.whats_next: Organisers demanded the government withdraw its plan and said the Sunday rally was only the beginning of the protests.
3485f8c799.blurb: More than 350,000 Czechs rallied in Prague against plans to scrap the fees that fund public broadcasters.
3485f8c799.spoken: Huge crowds filled Prague's Letná Plain on Sunday, with organisers saying more than 350,000 people turned out to defend Czech public television and radio. Many wore paper hats like Večerníček, the children's bedtime story mascot that became the protest's symbol. The government wants to scrap mandatory licence fees, worth 205 koruna, about seven pounds a month, and fund broadcasters from the state budget instead. Protesters say that would give ministers leverage over newsrooms, cutting budgets by around 15 per cent, and they point to Hungary, Poland, Serbia and Slovakia. The bill's first reading passed late at night in late October, sparking rallies and a staff strike. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš calls the criticism lies and hysterical, promising no interference in editorial work. His ANO party still polls around 30 per cent, but organisers say this is just the beginning.

4457075b0a.what_happened: Prince Harry made a surprise visit to Lviv, Ukraine, where he attended the National Invictus Games and a conference for medics. He met wounded veterans and watched adaptive sports competitions, including wheelchair rugby.
details: Prince Harry, a 42-year-old British royal, visited Lviv on Saturday for Ukraine’s National Invictus Games and a medics conference. The event was organized by Superhumans, a clinic specializing in rehabilitating war-wounded veterans.

Ukraine has about 1.4 million combat veterans, with more than 10 percent having disabilities. Harry, on his fourth trip since 2022, told veterans, 'You’re going to win the war,' and that they would be 'set up for success.'

The prince watched wheelchair rugby players competing for Ukraine’s team for the 2027 Invictus Games in Birmingham, England. Around 500 people registered to qualify for the 60-member squad, the largest ever planned.

Harry is the founder and patron of the Invictus Games Foundation, established in 2014 to support military personnel through adaptive sports. He hugged Valery Odainyk, a 41-year-old leg amputee and active serviceman, who said his sports involvement started with the Invictus Games.

The event was organized by Superhumans clinic for war-wounded rehabilitation.
Ukraine has 1.4 million veterans, over 10% with disabilities.
Harry said veterans will win the war and be set up for success.

4457075b0a.blurb: Prince Harry's surprise visit to Lviv boosts morale among Ukrainian veterans for the 2027 Invictus Games.
4457075b0a.spoken: Good morning, listeners! Prince Harry just made a surprise trip to Lviv, Ukraine, where he met with wounded veterans and medics. He attended the National Invictus Games and a conference organized by the Superhumans clinic, which helps injured soldiers recover. Ukraine has about 1.4 million combat veterans, and Harry told them they're going to win the war. He watched wheelchair rugby players competing for spots on the team for the 2027 Invictus Games in Birmingham, with 500 people trying out for 60 slots. Harry, who started the Invictus Games in 2014, even hugged a veteran named Valery Odainyk, who is still in the military despite having an amputated leg. This visit highlights ongoing support for Ukraine's veterans through sports.

3abfd7b66c.what_happened: A deep depression in the Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Monday (16) evening and develop into a severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday (17), according to the Department of Meteorology. The system was located about 640 km northeast of Trincomalee as of 11:30 p.m. Sunday and is moving away from Sri Lanka. Meanwhile, showers across Sri Lanka are expected to reduce from today.
details: The Department of Meteorology reports a deep depression in the Bay of Bengal that is likely to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Monday (16) evening and further develop into a severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday (17). As of 11:30 p.m. on Sunday, the system was approximately 640 km northeast of Trincomalee and is expected to continue moving away from Sri Lanka.

The Meteorology Department says prevailing showers across Sri Lanka are expected to reduce from today. Several spells of showers are forecast in the Western, Sabaragamuwa, North-western and Southern provinces, as well as the Kandy and Nuwara Eliya districts. Showers or thundershowers may occur at a few places in Uva Province and Ampara District after 2 p.m. Mainly dry weather is expected elsewhere, with misty conditions possible in many areas during the early morning.
The public has been advised to take precautions against temporary strong winds and lightning during thundershowers.

45cf407d6d.what_happened: The Sudanese Armed Forces launched an air strike that killed at least 13 civilians in the Abu Qalb area of West Kordofan. The victims included women and children, and several homes were destroyed.
details: The Sudanese Armed Forces, or SAF, launched an air strike. The strike killed at least 13 civilians in the Abu Qalb area of West Kordofan state, and the victims included women and children, according to the Emergency Lawyers rights group.

The warplanes from the military government attacked the Abu Zabad locality. The strike happened the day before Monday, and Emergency Lawyers said several homes were destroyed in the strike, which they described in a social media post on Monday after preliminary monitoring, but Al Jazeera was unable to immediately verify the report.

Emergency Lawyers said the continued use of indiscriminate airstrikes on residential areas poses a direct threat to civilian lives and is a grave violation of international humanitarian law. The group documents human rights violations and cited videos of horrific scenes of destruction. Mohamed Didan, the official spokesperson for the Special Operations Forces that fight alongside the SAF, said on Facebook that his troops moved through Abu Zabad and eliminated RSF positions in West Kordofan.

The war between the army and the RSF began in April 2023 and has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, according to several aid organisations. Reports say the war has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced about 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine, while much fighting is concentrated in Darfur and Kordofan and recently shifted towards the Blue Nile province. Drone warfare has surged during the war and become the deadliest threat to civilians, experts said both sides are being supplied with drones by countries in the Middle East and beyond, and the SAF has gained control over several strategically important villages and localities in West Kordofan recently.
key_facts: Sudanese army warplanes killed at least 13 civilians in West Kordofan.
Victims included women and children, several homes destroyed.
Emergency Lawyers said airstrike was grave legal violation.

45cf407d6d.blurb: Sudanese army air attack in West Kordofan killed 13 civilians including women and children.
45cf407d6d.spoken: Here is the scene. A war is still going on in Sudan. The army there used warplanes in an air strike. The strike hit the Abu Zabad area in West Kordofan. It killed at least thirteen civilians. The victims included women and children. A local rights group called Emergency Lawyers said several homes were destroyed. They said the continued use of airstrikes on homes is a threat to civilian lives and breaks international law. The army's special operations forces also said they moved through the area and removed what they called RSF positions. The wider war began in April twenty twenty three. It has caused a big humanitarian crisis. Reports say it has killed at least fifty-nine thousand people and displaced about thirteen million.
